title: It’s Not Just a Notification
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Kirschner uses a 2026 experiment by Fournier and colleagues (180 students, a Stroop task, realistic pop-up notifications) to argue that phone notifications measurably slow cognitive processing for about seven seconds, even when students stay on task and make no more errors. He stresses that the cost is invisible in a classroom: a student appears to be participating while losing processing capacity and the thread of thought. He reframes the school phone debate away from total screen time toward the number and frequency of interruptions, noting participants averaged over 150 notifications and 100 checks a day. Drawing on work on attention contagion, he adds that other pupils' screens and notifications impose a shared cost on the whole room. His policy conclusion is practical: notifications off during instruction and independent work, phones off the desk or in lockers, and the reasons explained to students in terms of working memory. Close call between Learning & Curriculum and Ed-Tech; filed as Ed-Tech because the notification and school phone policy is the actual subject.
points: Notifications slow processing for about seven seconds even when no error appears, so lost attention in a classroom can be invisible.
The size of the disruption tracked notification volume and checking frequency rather than total screen time, which shifts the school policy question from hours to interruptions.
Impersonal notifications and a neighbour's lit-up screen also disrupt attention, so distraction is contagious and off-task screens are a collective problem.
Recommended school measures are notifications off in instruction and independent work, phones off the table or in lockers, with the working-memory rationale explained to students.
Kirschner concedes the evidence is a lab Stroop task rather than a classroom study, but argues the effect on simple tasks implies larger losses on demanding ones.
quotes: In simple tasks, such a disruption shows up as a small delay. In complex tasks, recovery can take much longer.

The conclusion: notifications draw attention through three different routes at once. First, through salience: something suddenly appears in your visual field and stands out, pulling attention towards it.
The damage is often not visible as chaos, but invisible loss of processing capacity. And we have far less of that than we like to think.

This study shows something that’s at least as interesting for schools and educators: not only screen time matters, but also the number and frequency of interruptions. The size of the disruption was related to notification volume and checking frequency, not simply to total time on the device.

The participating students spent, on average, almost seven hours per day on their phones, received more than 150 notifications per day, and checked their phones more than 100 times per day. These are no longer occasional interruptions. This is a constant rhythm of interruption.

What matters here is understanding that attention is not a purely individual state. Just like yawning, attention in a classroom is social: students can strengthen one another’s attention, but they can also spread one another’s inattention.

The conclusion for education is fairly simple, but apparently still controversial: anyone who wants students to learn must protect their attention. Not in a totalitarian way. Not hysterically. Just professionally.
